newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's corporate problems swell on Kia woes.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's corporate problems swell on Kia woes.

text.p: South Korea's corporate crisis deepened on Tuesday as the stricken Kia Group received emergency loans until creditors could formalise a rescue plan and rumours hammered the sixth-ranked Ssangyong Group.

Fuelling the sense of crisis was news that creditors of the troubled Jinro Group would not extend its bail-out benefits beyond Sunday's expiry date, even though the conglomerate's troubles were far from over.
Analysts said the move would eventually result in Jinro's default because lead non-banking financial institutions would call in their loan payments.
Seoul share prices plunged on fears that the chain of corporate collapses could only grow, analysts said.
Kia Group said it would cut the number of its domestic affiliates to 13 by merging and selling units, and raise 3.1 trillion won ($3.45 billion) by selling real estate in a self-rescue attempt.

In a dramatic move, creditor banks agreed on Tuesday to extend 160 billion won in emergency loans to Kia to keep it in business until a bank anti-bankruptcy committee could formally adopt a rescue plan, the Korea First Bank said.
As a condition for additional loans to Kia, creditors would ask the current management to relinquish their management rights.
But analysts said Kia's self-rescue package to slim down and sell off assets amounted to a temporary bandage.
"Kia has the wrong management. Unless the management is changed, Kia's turnaround looks unlikely," said Rhee Namuh, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine.
Kia's woes combined with rumours of cash flow problems in the Ssangyong Group roiled Seoul stock and currency markets as nervous investors dumped shares.
A Ssangyong spokesman strongly denied the group was in trouble. "That's just a vicious, groundless rumour that is going around," he said.
The dollar soared to 894.50 won after opening at 892.40. It closed at 894.40. Dealers said jitters about Ssangyong sparked speculative dollar buying.
The composite stock index lost 2.0 percent, or 14.95 points, to close at 725.98. All 10 listed Ssangyong Group shares fell to their daily lower limit.

"Investors are increasingly concerned Ssangyong will follow Kia's suit as rumours say creditors are expected to put the group into the bail-out scheme," said Cha Hee-gun, broker at Sunkyong Securities.
"If it is true, the group is in really serious financial trouble."
Wee Sung-bok, executive vice president at Ssangyong's major creditor Chohung Bank, also denied the rumours.
"There have been no such applications from Ssangyong and we have no plan to put the group under the bail-out committee at all," Wee said.

South Korean banks in April formed a committee to keep afloat promising companies staggered by heavy debts. Under the banks' bail-out agreement, the credit lines of companies designated for rescue would remain open, even after they defaulted on debt payments.
The first beneficiary of the agreement was the Jinro Group, the country's 19th largest conglomerate, which has been burdened by some 3.2 trillion won of debt.
But creditor banks on Tuesday said they would not extend the bail-out period for Jinro beyond Sunday's expiry.
"The bail-out period of Jinro Group will expire on July 27 as scheduled," said Ku Ja-yong, director and deputy president of Commercial Bank.
"Instead, we are planning to suggest extending the period of principal payments and reducing interest payments in order to help the group survive," he said.
